**Paragraph 1 — Identity & Significance**: 

Pope Alexander III, born Roland, was the head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 7 September 1159 until his death in 1181. He was a member of the House of Hohenstaufen and succeeded his predecessor, Pope Adrian IV, on 7 September 1159. His papacy was marked by conflicts with the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I and the growth of the Papal States.

**Paragraph 2 — What Happened**: 

During his papacy, Alexander III played a significant role in the investiture controversy, a conflict between the Catholic Church and the Holy Roman Empire over the appointment of bishops and the exercise of papal authority. He also clashed with Frederick I, who was attempting to limit papal power. The conflict led to the First Crusade and the establishment of the Catholic Church's temporal authority.

**Paragraph 3 — Legacy & Consequence**: 

Alexander III's papacy had significant consequences for European history. The Investiture Controversy led to the growth of the Papal States, which became a major power in Italy. The conflict also led to the First Crusade, which had a profound impact on the Middle East and the development of Christianity. The legacy of Alexander III can also be seen in the rise of the Holy Roman Empire, which would eventually become a dominant force in European politics.

**Closing**: 

The papacy of Alexander III marked a significant turning point in the relationship between the Catholic Church and the Holy Roman Empire. His conflicts with Frederick I and the growth of the Papal States would have far-reaching consequences for European history.
